pages.name: M2 — run it from the browser

artboards.title: R1 · Who walked away, with the way out
R1 · A problem in full, with the check

annotations.text:
M1 is read-only: every screen here reads what the SQLite store already holds, so nothing on the canvas needs a write path.

The design rule: one navigation, no role switch, no expert mode. Prose carries what we found; monospace carries how we know. Start at 'How the screens connect'.

The trace viewer is live on the canvas — click any step in the left column and the right pane follows it.

The band at the top is the thing nothing else in this category has: what she walked back in remembering.

This is where the two audiences look at the same thing for different reasons. The quotes and the cost are for the product owner; the four calls on the right are for the developer. Neither is hidden behind a mode.
Memory is per run and per agent, so this panel is empty on a fresh run and is the whole story by visit three. It is what makes 'she came back and she is still annoyed' visible.

Settled: authored config — targets, personas, populations, guardrails — lives in the database from M2, because this is where people will be setting it up anyway. YAML becomes import and export.

That is what these three screens are drawn for: a saved record with a saved-at time, a persona that knows which populations use it, and a rename that cannot break an agent id.
Watching a run is the same trace viewer as M1 with a live cursor, not a second component. The only additions are the 'happening now' row, the people panel on the left, and the feed on the right.
The estimate is the thing that makes a product owner willing to press the button at all. It is worked out from the average cost of a visit on the last run, so it is honest about being a range.

R1 closes the loop: you change something, you send the same people back, and they tell you whether it worked.

These are drawn on main as of 98b1b43 — cohorts, simulations, named people — in the rail and the components Nick wrote, with one addition: a 'Who came back' item after 'Who walked away'. That pair is promise and verdict.

Start here, then read 'Who came back'.

The screen this slice is for. A named person's own account of whether the fix won them back leads; the signature diff is demoted to a panel at the foot, under the caveat Compare.tsx already carries.

Tomás is the reason for that order. The signature he filed this time keys differently from the one he filed last time, so the comparison counts the old one as gone and his new one as new — while he is plainly describing one problem. Read as machine output it says fixed; read as a person it says not fixed. He is right.

Entry one. The promise — 'Priya said a fix would bring them back' — is already on this screen on main and nothing acts on it. The band under her is the act.

It says plainly that everybody goes, because the API cannot carry back a subset (StartExecutionBodySchema takes a parent id and nothing else).

Entry two, and it is at the FOOT of the page on purpose. The offer to check a fix follows the evidence and the triage decision rather than competing with them: you read what happened, you mark it fixed, and then the page asks whether you want to find out.

The free-text box is the existing `reason` field on the start body. Nothing new is needed on the API for any of this.

The only place in the product where the difference between carrying forward and running again can actually be read, so it is spelled out here rather than in a tooltip: a clean execution asks whether a stranger hits the problem, carrying forward asks whether the person who left is satisfied.

Who goes, what they keep, what it will cost, and what is left on today's ceiling.
